sorting network merges are constrained by the 0-1 input lattice structure, which may impose irreducible comparison costs that 3-way merging cannot reduce.","Strassen reduces asymptotic complexity; here we seek a constant-factor improvement of exactly one comparator, which is a much finer-grained and harder target."],"overturn_conditions":["If exhaustive search over all 3-way merge networks of (4,4,5) shows none costs \u226425, the analogy does not help here even if it holds in general.","If the information-theoretic lower bound for merging (4,4,5) already exceeds 25, the analogy to Strassen-style savings is misleading for this specific problem."],"shared_structure":["Both 3-way merge sorting and Strassen-style divide-and-conquer decompose a problem into smaller independent subproblems solved in parallel, then combine results.","In both, the key question is whether the combination step can be done more cheaply by combining all parts at once rather than sequentially in pairs.","Both exploit that pairwise-sequential combination introduces redundant work that a simultaneous combination can avoid."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_001"],"transfer_claims":["The general principle \u2014 that combining k subproblems simultaneously can be cheaper than k-1 sequential pairwise combinations \u2014 transfers from matrix multiplication to sorting network merges.","The methodology of searching for the combination primitive empirically (testing all 2^13 vectors) transfers directly from the verification protocol."]},"claim":"A 44-comparator 13-input sorting network likely exists and would be discoverable via a 3-way merge decomposition: independently sort subsequences of sizes 4, 4, and 5 (cost 5+5+9=19 comparators), then merge the three sorted runs with a custom 3-way merge costing at most 25 comparators, yielding total \u2264 44. The reason search stalls at 45 is that standard pairwise-merge decompositions (e.g., 6+7 or 12+1) inherently require more merge comparators than a 3-way merge that exploits simultaneous cross-run comparisons.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If every possible 3-way merge network for sorted runs of lengths (4,4,5) requires 26 or more comparators, this decomposition cannot yield 44 and the conjecture fails.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If S(13)=45 is provably optimal via exhaustive SAT-based search (analogous to the n=9,10 proofs), then no 44-comparator network exists regardless of decomposition strategy.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If alternative decompositions like (3,5,5) or (3,4,6) consistently yield lower merge costs under the same 3-way scheme, the specific (4,4,5) decomposition is not the right attack point and the claim's specificity is wrong.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 3-way merge primitive offers no advantage over two sequential pairwise merges for all tested sub-run sizes at n=13, the structural hypothesis explaining why search stalls at 45 is incorrect.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Pairwise merge of sorted runs a+b then (a+b)+c applies two sequential merge networks. For 4+4+5: pairwise would sort 4+4\u21928 (merge cost m(4,4)) then merge 8+5\u219213 (merge cost m(8,5)), where m(8,5) alone likely exceeds 20. A 3-way merge can interleave comparators across all three runs at once: a comparator between run-A[i] and run-B[j] can simultaneously inform placement relative to run-C via shared structure, reducing redundant comparisons. If the 3-way merge of (4,4,5) achieves \u226425 comparators \u2014 plausible because 3-way merging has lower information-theoretic depth than two sequential pairwise merges \u2014 the total 19+25=44 beats 45. The 0-1 principle enables exact verification of any such candidate in milliseconds.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
